title: Addition polymers and disposal; Alcohols: production, dehydration and halogenation
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR14#t1 term and clue written for the game; OR14#t3 term and clue written for the game; OR14#t4 term and clue written for the game; OR14#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: OR14#N.3, OR16#N.4, OR14#N.5, OR16#N.7, OR14#N.8, OR16#N.11, OR14#N.13, OR16#N.18a, OR14#N.16.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Polymer
items.clue: A very long molecule made of many small molecules joined by covalent bonds.

items.label: Repeating unit
items.clue: Section with two main-chain carbons and extension bonds at each end, e.g. –CH₂–CHCl–.

items.label: Intermolecular forces
items.clue: Attractions between neighbouring chains, overcome on heating so that a plastic softens.

items.label: Monomer
items.clue: Small molecule with a C=C, such as ethene or CH₂=CHCl, that joins with many others into a long chain.

questions.stem: Propene, CH₂=CHCH₃, forms the addition polymer poly(propene), written as [repeating unit]ₙ. Which option gives the repeating unit and describes it correctly?

options.text: –CH₂=CH(CH₃)–, keeping each monomer's C=C
–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–, one unit of a single long chain
–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–, all three carbons in the main chain
CH₃CH₂CH₃, one of n separate small molecules

questions.explanation: One bond of each C=C breaks and the two former C=C carbons form the main chain, with CH₃ as a side group. [–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–]ₙ represents one chain containing n of these units.

questions.stem: Ethanol is made either by fermentation, C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g), or by hydration of ethene, C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g). Which statement about the two routes is correct? Ar: H 1.0; C 12.0; O 16.0

options.text: A higher percentage yield in fermentation would raise its atom economy closer to hydration's.
Fermentation has the lower atom economy, so more of its reactant mass becomes by-product.
Hydration has an atom economy of 100%, so a hydration plant produces no waste of any kind.
Only about a quarter of the reactant mass in fermentation ends up in ethanol (atom economy 25.6%).

questions.stem: A section of an addition polymer is –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–. Which is the monomer?

options.text: (CH₃)₃CH
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃
(CH₃)₃COH
(CH₃)₂C=CH₂

questions.explanation: The repeating unit is –CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–. Restoring the C=C between the two main-chain carbons gives (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene.

questions.stem: A fuel company says its bioethanol, made by fermenting sugar from sugar cane, is "carbon neutral". Which statement best evaluates the claim?

options.text: It is not fully justified: the cane absorbed the CO₂ that burning releases, but fossil fuels used to farm, transport and distil the ethanol add CO₂.
It is justified: the cane takes in CO₂ as it grows, so no net CO₂ is ever added to the air.
It is justified: fermentation absorbs as much CO₂ as burning the ethanol releases.
It is not justified, because ethanol forms more CO₂ per mole burned than petrol does.

questions.stem: Why does adding a plasticiser make PVC flexible?

options.text: Its molecules sit between the chains and weaken the forces between them.
It breaks some of the C–Cl bonds, so the chains become non-polar.
It forms covalent cross-links between the chains, and these act like hinges.
It makes the chains much longer, so each chain bends more easily.

questions.explanation: Pushing chains apart weakens the dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces between them, so the chains can move past each other.

questions.stem: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid. How many different alkenes can form?
questions.explanation: Losing H from C1 gives but-1-ene. Losing H from C3 gives but-2-ene, as both E and Z isomers.

questions.stem: A council burns mixed plastic waste, including PVC, to generate electricity. Which extra step deals with the main problem caused by burning the PVC?

options.text: Sorting out the PVC first and sending it to landfill instead, as it cannot be burned
Passing the waste gases through a base to remove the hydrogen chloride formed
Burning the plastics with less air, so that less carbon dioxide forms
Cooling the waste gases, so that the chlorine condenses and can be collected

questions.explanation: The chlorine in PVC ends up as HCl, a toxic, acidic gas. A base such as calcium oxide neutralises it before the gases are released.

questions.stem: Two reactions both need acid: (1) cyclohexanol, heated with concentrated phosphoric acid → cyclohexene + water (2) 2-methylpropan-2-ol, shaken with concentrated hydrochloric acid → 2-chloro-2-methylpropane + water What does the H⁺ do in both reactions?

options.text: It acts as a nucleophile and bonds to the carbon atom carrying the OH group.
It pulls the OH group off as a hydroxide ion, OH⁻, which then leaves.
It bonds to the O of the OH group, so the C–O bond breaks and water leaves.
It removes a hydrogen atom from a C–H bond first, so that the OH group then falls off.

questions.explanation: Protonation turns –OH into –OH₂⁺. Neutral water is a good leaving group. Then H⁺ is lost (1) or Cl⁻ bonds to the carbon (2).

questions.stem: Poly(propene) can be heated until soft, moulded into a new shape, and cooled. The same plastic can be remoulded many times, and its chemical properties do not change. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Heating breaks C–C bonds in the chains, and new C–C bonds form in the new positions on cooling.
Heating turns the chains back into propene molecules, which polymerise again as the plastic cools.
Heating overcomes the forces between chains, which re-form on cooling; no covalent bonds break.
Heating breaks the covalent bonds between neighbouring chains, and these re-form on cooling.
